source.title: The Bail Project, Annual Report 2024 (fiscal year July 2023 to June 2024)
source.quote: Florida is the only state that requires the automatic deduction of fines and fees from bail payments.

rows.explainer: Bail not returned is either forfeited after a missed date (the county's gain) or kept for the client's fines and fees, which the client would otherwise owe (the client's gain). Clients make 92% of their dates and forfeiture usually follows several misses, while Florida deducts fees from every bail: our judgment, half (20% to 80%). rows.label: Share of bailed-out clients who would have lost their housing in detention

source.title: Sandra Susan Smith (2022), How Pretrial Incarceration Diminishes Individuals' Employment Prospects, Federal Probation 86(3)
source.quote: including legal debt (36 percent), missed work (40 percent), lost jobs (18 percent), and lost property (18 percent)
source.note: New York City Criminal Justice Agency survey of people held pretrial; the charity's 2023 report says 7% of clients reported no stable housing at release.

rows.explainer: Among New Yorkers held pretrial 18% lost jobs and 18% lost property, the share rising with days held. Our judgment: 5% of clients held for weeks would lose a home (1% to 12%). Jobs lost are in the shared earnings gain of release, so this counts only the home. Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Validity of the shared release effects for The Bail Project's clients

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Prison Policy Initiative's decarceration branch (dec_evidence_adj 0.75)

rows.explainer: The case-outcome and earnings effects are quasi-experiments on marginal defendants in Philadelphia, Miami and Harris County a decade ago, and the mortality figure comes from New York parolees; the charity's clients are people a judge set bail for that they couldn't pay, many like the marginal defendants. 0.75 (0.5 to 0.95), as Prison Policy Initiative's decarceration branch. The doubt about the reach and days counted is in their own ranges and the missing-data discount, not here. Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Leverage and funging of The Bail Project's bail

source.title: charityevals' judgment for charitable bail

rows.explainer: Families, bondsmen's 10% fees and other bail funds would pay some of the bail the charity pays, and its bailouts free local funds' money for others; no government pays bail, and the charity's grants to partner funds are in its cost. Our judgment: 0.94 (0.83 to 1.02). Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Side effect: children and partners spared a parent's detention, as a share of the value

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Prison Policy Initiative's ue_dec_family (15% for prison terms, Wakefield and Wildeman 2013)

rows.explainer: Most clients are parents or carers; a parent jailed for weeks costs children care and income. Prison Policy Initiative's model counts 15% for longer prison terms; for weeks in jail 10% (0 to 30%). Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Side effect: crime by people released before trial, net of crime later avoided, as a share of the value

source.title: Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2016), NBER Working Paper 22511
source.quote: Pre-trial release also increases the likelihood of rearrest prior to case disposition by 7.6 percentage points

rows.explainer: Released defendants are rearrested more before their case closes but show 'no detectable effects' on crime up to four years later (Dobbie et al.); in Harris County detention raises later crime (Heaton et al. 2017). The reference class is Prison Policy Initiative's ue_dec_crime, -10% (-30% to 0) for people kept out of prison, where the years outside are years of risk; here the time out is weeks and later crime is unchanged, so -5% (-20% to +5%). Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Share of the pretrial detention The Bail Project counts as prevented that clients would really have served without it

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2016), NBER Working Paper 22511
source.quote: the mean three day release rate of 55.2 percentage points

rows.explainer: We read the charity's days prevented as gross: the days clients would have been held had nobody paid, with no deduction for release by other means, which is counted only here. Without the charity some clients would have been bailed by family, a bondsman's 10% fee, another bail fund or a judge's review, and some would have pleaded guilty to get out. Over half of defendants are out within three days (Dobbie et al.), so people still held when the charity steps in are the ones who stay: 60% of the days (35% to 95%, the high end if the charity's count is already net). Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.

rows.label: Days in jail after a missed court date (warrant, arrest, hold)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Science News on Fishbane, Ouss and Shah (2020), Behavioral nudges reduce failure to appear for court, Science 370

rows.explainer: A missed date brings a bench warrant; many are arrested on it and held a few days before being seen. Our judgment: 5 days (1 to 20), the short holds after warrant arrests in the New York trial's setting. Read by both of charityevals' Bail Project models.
